cards.text: This one's labeled a song for the Sabbath day, and the songwriter is singing it straight to the LORD, the Most High. He skips the warmup and opens with this: it is good to praise the LORD and to sing praises to His name. Not "fine," not "if you've got a minute," but GOOD.

cards.question: The songwriter proclaims the LORD's loving devotion in the morning and His faithfulness at ___.

cards.text: And he wants music behind it: the ten-stringed harp and the melody of the lyre. TEN strings, friend, and I can't work ONE mustache without knocking over the sprinkles.

cards.question: Then the songwriter gives the reason behind all this singing. He says the LORD has made him glad. By what?
True or false: the songwriter says the LORD's works are great and His thoughts are deep.

cards.text: Then he says there's something a senseless man doesn't know and a fool doesn't understand, and it's about the wicked. Whenever somebody starts a sentence with "a fool doesn't understand," I check my own apron FIRST.

cards.question: The wicked sprout like grass and all evildoers flourish, and the songwriter says they will be forever ___.

cards.text: Then, right in the middle of the song, comes the shortest line of all: "But You, O LORD, are exalted forever!" Grass versus FOREVER, friend, and I'm not putting a single sprinkle on the grass.

cards.question: True or false: the songwriter says the LORD's enemies will come out on top in the end.

cards.text: Then it gets personal: the LORD has exalted the songwriter's horn like that of a wild ox, and he's been anointed with fine oil. Not a petting zoo goat, friend, a WILD OX.

cards.question: Next the songwriter talks about what he sees and hears. What does he say his own eyes see?

answers.text: The LORD's glory in the temple
A great harvest in the land

cards.text: And his ears hear the wailing of his wicked foes. Eyes AND ears, friend, the man is getting this news in SURROUND SOUND.

cards.question: If the wicked are like grass, what does the songwriter say the righteous will flourish like?

cards.text: A palm tree, AND they'll grow like a cedar in Lebanon, planted in the house of the LORD and flourishing in the courts of our God. That's not a potted plant on a windowsill, friend, that tree has a permanent ADDRESS.

cards.question: True or false: the songwriter says the righteous stop bearing fruit once they reach old age.

cards.text: Nope, in old age they still bear fruit, and they stay healthy and green. My edges went soft and blurry after years of baking on the Millers' counter, friend, so I'm hugging this verse with my WHOLE mustache.

cards.question: The song ends with the righteous still flourishing in old age, still speaking up about the LORD. What does the songwriter say they'll proclaim?

answers.text: The LORD is upright and is their Rock
The LORD is gentle and is their Shepherd
The LORD is merciful and is their Light

cards.text: And the very last line: "The LORD is upright; He is my Rock, and in Him there is no unrighteousness." Not one crumb of it, friend, and I have NEVER pulled a batch out of the oven that clean.

findings.problem: Stop 1, card 6 quotes "a fool doesn't understand", which isn't the exact BSB wording.

rule.text: Quotes: Quotation marks around Bible words mean the exact BSB wording, punctuation included.

findings.problem: The card says that what the senseless man and fool do not understand is "about the wicked," but that detail comes from verse 7. The card cites only verse 6; it should cite Psalm 92:6-7.

rule.text: Cite exactly what the card uses. Every story card cites the verses it tells, from the first verse it uses to the last, no wider and no narrower.

findings.problem: The question replaces the psalm's concessive "though" with "and," losing the contrast between the wicked flourishing and their eventual destruction. The contrast should remain while the outcome stays blank.
